red_flags: Spreading perineal erythema, crepitus, or systemic toxicity — necrotizing perineal infection; urgent surgical referral
Throbbing anal pain with fever and inability to sit — perianal or ischiorectal abscess; urgent surgical referral
Hard, ulcerated, or non-healing lesion — especially a 'fissure' off the midline — anal carcinoma until biopsied
Perianal sepsis in a diabetic or immunosuppressed patient — deteriorates fast
Urinary retention with perianal pain — deep pelvic sepsis
exam: Position the patient and inspect the anal margin in good light — skin tags, external fistula opening, warts, ulcer, or a blue-purple tender lump
Part the buttocks gently — a posterior midline tear with a sentinel tag is a fissure; note if the tear is lateral (atypical — think carcinoma or Crohn's)
Palpate around the margin for induration, warmth, and fluctuance — an abscess may show only deep tenderness
Feel for a cord-like tract running from an external opening toward the anus — fistula
Perform a digital rectal exam if tolerated — defer it in an obvious acute fissure and record why
On rectal exam: assess sphincter tone, feel for induration, an internal fistula opening, or a hard mass
Proctoscopy where tolerated — internal hemorrhoids and their degree
Inspect the natal cleft for midline pits and a discharging sinus — pilonidal disease, not anal disease
Palpate inguinal lymph nodes — anal carcinoma drains to the groin
Record temperature and examine the abdomen — tenderness or a mass supports Crohn's disease

investigations.why: Leukocytosis supports abscess; anemia supports Crohn's disease or an occult carcinoma over hemorrhoids and fissure
Recurrent or severe perianal sepsis is often the first presentation of diabetes
Raised values support active sepsis or Crohn's disease; normal values fit fissure, hemorrhoids, and warts
Confirms internal hemorrhoids as the bleeding source and excludes a low rectal lesion the finger missed

investigations.test: Biopsy of any atypical ulcer, lateral fissure, or mass
investigations.why: The only way to separate anal carcinoma from chronic fissure, Crohn's ulceration, and viral lesions
Second-line — if a fistula is recurrent or complex, or perianal Crohn's is suspected: maps the tracts and any hidden collection before referral
